props.text: CONFIDENTIAL  —  PREPARED FOR MERIDIAN FINANCIAL GROUP
A phased move of Meridian Financial Group from its Fairfax data centre to AWS, costed, sequenced and underwritten by a fixed-price commitment for each phase.

cells.content: The commitment, the headline numbers and the objectives they serve
What the February audit found, and the compliance gaps it opened
Target architecture and the three phases that reach it
One-off cost, annual run rate, and the point the two curves cross
The six risks that could move the date, and what holds each one down
The discovery sprint, and what Meridian owes it
Accounts, VPCs, Direct Connect, identity federation, guardrails
Oracle RAC to Aurora PostgreSQL, including two rewritten PL/SQL packages
The 34 services on the vSphere estate, containerised onto Fargate
CloudWatch, X-Ray and the four dashboards the platform team asked for
Run-books, four training sessions, thirty days of shadow support

props.text: Out of scope: application code changes beyond replatforming, the retail mobile client, and the Fairfax facility exit itself. Each can be quoted separately once the wave plan is agreed.
Why Meridian should move this year

Meridian runs regulated workloads on hardware that leaves support inside eighteen months. The refresh has to be funded either way; spending it on a migration instead buys back the operating model as well as the capacity.

Three of the five core systems reach end of support before December 2026, and the Oracle RAC cluster that carries settlement is the oldest of them. Server utilisation sits at 87% of critical capacity, monthly downtime runs 23 hours against a 4-hour SLA, and each new environment takes six to eight weeks to provision. Three product launches slipped in 2025 for that reason alone.

We propose a three-phase migration to AWS built on managed services, executed with zero planned downtime for customer-facing systems using blue-green cutovers and automated rollback. **Each phase is fixed-price**, and each ends at a checkpoint Meridian can stop at without stranding the work already done.

items: Retire the $2.1M four-year hardware refresh and move the spend to operating expenditure.
Cut environment provisioning from six weeks to under fifteen minutes.
Reach SOC 2 Type II on automated evidence collection rather than quarterly manual attestation.
Give the eleven engineering teams isolated environments and their own delivery pipelines.
Establish multi-region disaster recovery with a recovery point objective under one minute.

props.text: **Our commitment.** If any phase exceeds its quoted price, Apex absorbs the difference. If a cutover wave misses its window, we roll back inside the same maintenance window and re-run it at our cost.
Two engineers spent two weeks on site in February 2026, instrumenting the estate and interviewing the platform, security and settlement teams. The findings below are measured, not estimated.
On systems past end of support
The Catalyst stack passed end of support in June 2025 and is running on a lapsed contract.

items: **Capital.** The refresh cycle needs $2.1M every four years. The next one is already six months overdue, and $1.8M of it falls in FY2027.
**Speed.** Hardware procurement adds six to eight weeks to any capacity change. Three product launches slipped in 2025 waiting on it.
**Recovery.** Disaster recovery is tested once a year. The November 2025 test showed a 4-hour data gap and a 12-hour recovery time against a 1-hour target.
**Security.** Forty-seven unpatched critical vulnerabilities sit on systems that no longer receive vendor fixes.

props.text: Meridian holds SOC 2 Type I and is committed to Type II by Q1 2027. Four control families do not currently produce the evidence a Type II audit needs.

The gap that matters is not encryption or logging in themselves — Meridian does both today. It is that the evidence has to be assembled by hand each quarter, by the same four people who run the platform. A Type II audit samples continuously, and a quarterly export cannot answer it.

From phase 1 the audit account receives CloudTrail, Config and Inspector findings on an immutable, cross-account trail. The evidence an auditor asks for is a query rather than a project, and the four people go back to running the platform.

**Regulatory notification.** Meridian files an FCA material outsourcing notification in week 2. Apex prepares the submission pack; Meridian signs it. Nothing moves to AWS before that notification is acknowledged.
The target, and the road to it
Managed services wherever a managed service exists. Meridian keeps the application logic and hands back the operational burden of everything underneath it.

props.text: **Figure 2.** Twenty-six weeks, three phases, four cutover waves.
Establish the landing zone before anything moves: a multi-account organisation, network topology, identity federation and the guardrails that make the later phases boring.

items: Control Tower organisation with separate production, staging and audit accounts.
VPC design with Transit Gateway, and a 10 Gbps Direct Connect to Fairfax.
Identity federation against Meridian’s existing Entra ID tenant.
Service control policies, Config rules and CloudTrail to an immutable log archive.
Terraform modules and the CI pipeline that applies them.

props.text: Databases first, application tier behind them, in four cutover waves ordered by blast radius. Each wave rehearses against staging before it touches production.

cells.content: Parallel run for two cycles, then switch

props.text: Right-size against four weeks of real production metrics rather than the sizing assumptions made in week one, then hand the platform over.

items: Instance right-sizing against observed load, with Compute Savings Plans on the stable base.
S3 lifecycle policies moving cold settlement archives to Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Multi-region failover drill, executed with Meridian’s own on-call rota.
Run-book handover, four training sessions, and thirty days of shadow support.

props.text: The programme is deliberately light on Meridian effort — a total of roughly 0.5 full-time equivalents across twenty-six weeks, concentrated around the cutover waves.

cells.content: Two half-days a week; decision authority on architecture
Four days in weeks 15–19, for parallel-run reconciliation
One day a fortnight; owns the FCA notification and the audit account
Attends each of the four cutover go / no-go reviews

props.text: What it costs, and when it pays back
One-off migration cost of $486,000 against an annual saving of $1,142,000. The curves cross in month six of the first full year of operation.
Oracle and VMware licensing disappears entirely: Aurora PostgreSQL and Fargate carry no separate licence. Platform operations falls by 1.5 FTE, redeployed rather than removed.
Six risks carry enough weight to change the plan. Each has a named owner at Apex, a trigger that surfaces it early, and a response rehearsed before the wave it threatens.

cells.content: Change data capture with continuous validation; parallel run for two settlement cycles before switch
Every wave rehearsed twice against staging; rollback scripted and timed under 40 minutes
Feature audit completed in discovery; two PL/SQL packages rewritten ahead of wave 3
FCA notification filed in week 2; audit account and evidence pipeline live from phase 1
Named deputies for all four Apex roles; Meridian effort capped at 0.5 FTE per week
Budget alarms at 80% and 95%; savings plans committed only after four weeks of real metrics

props.text: Until wave 4 completes, the Fairfax estate stays live and reconciled. Any wave can be reversed inside its own maintenance window, and reversal is rehearsed alongside the cutover it undoes. Meridian is never in a position where stopping means starting again.

items: The February inventory is complete: 34 services, 3 databases, 48 TB of primary storage.
Direct Connect is provisioned by week 4. A delay here moves every subsequent wave.
The two PL/SQL packages identified in discovery are the only Oracle-specific code in scope.
Meridian retains its Entra ID tenant; no identity provider migration is included.
Cutover windows fall on the Saturday nights already reserved for planned maintenance.

props.text: If any assumption proves wrong during the discovery sprint, we re-price before phase 1 begins rather than raising a change request halfway through it.
We recommend a two-week discovery sprint in May 2026. It produces the artefacts phase 1 consumes, and it prices the rest of the programme to the dollar.

items: Sign the discovery sprint statement of work — two weeks, $48,000, fixed.
Nominate a technical lead and a settlement expert, at 0.5 FTE each.
Provide read-only access to vCenter, the Oracle estate and the network inventory.
Attend the architecture workshop in week 1 and the findings review in week 2.
Approve the phase 1 statement of work, priced from the sprint.

props.text: **Elena Vasquez** — Principal Cloud Architect, Apex Consulting
